title: America's draft lottery
photoNote: Secretary of War Henry L. Stimson, blindfolded, draws the first capsule of the 1940 draft lottery as President Roosevelt watches from the microphones, Washington, 29 October 1940. Harris and Ewing Collection, Library of Congress, public domain (no known restrictions). Supplied by Brian 24 Oct 2026; replaced the Berryman cartoon (NARA 6012221), which still appears in the Story Card.
body:
A blindfolded man reached into a giant glass bowl in Washington, and millions of young American men waited to hear their number.

29 October 1940. Two weeks after registration day, the government drew the lottery for America's first peacetime draft. Every registered man had a number. Now the order they would be called in came out of a bowl last used for the draft of the First World War.

Secretary of War Henry Stimson, blindfolded, pulled out the first capsule. President Franklin D. Roosevelt read the number aloud: 158.

Families listened on the radio, and newspapers printed every number as fast as it came in. Cartoonist Clifford Berryman drew the scene that day with Mars, the god of war, at the bowl and Uncle Sam waiting his turn.

The men called that winter expected to serve one year. Thirteen months later came Pearl Harbor.

declassified.fact: The ceremony was packed with relics. The capsules were stirred with a wooden ladle said to be cut from a rafter of Independence Hall in Philadelphia, and 500 veterans of the First World War escorted them to the auditorium. Outside, warplanes flew past while Roosevelt spoke.
